issues.legal_issue: A tenant whose defence against delivery of possession has been struck out may participate in the landlord’s case only to a limited extent and subject to the court’s discretion.
material_facts: A landlord brought a suit seeking possession of premises from a tenant.
The tenant filed a written statement, but its defence was later struck out after a failure to comply with rent-deposit requirements.
The validity of the order striking out the defence was final and was not in issue.
The dispute concerned whether the tenant could cross-examine the landlord’s witnesses and address arguments based on the landlord’s case.
issues.conclusion: The tenant may generally cross-examine the landlord’s witnesses and address arguments based on the landlord’s case, subject to the court’s discretion to prevent prejudice to the landlord. The tenant may not lead evidence of its own, and cross-examination must be confined to identifying falsity or weaknesses in the landlord’s case rather than presenting the tenant’s own defence.
issues.legal_principle: The consequence under section 17(3) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956, is a punitive provision and must be strictly construed, with the tenant’s disabilities limited to what justice requires. The plaintiff must still prove the case, and the tenant’s limited participation can assist the court in testing the plaintiff’s evidence. The court must guard against prejudice and may restrict or exclude cross-examination where appropriate. The Court relied on the general procedural principles in Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah, Paradise Industrial Corpn. v. Kiln Plastics Products, and Babbar Sewing Machine Company v. Trilok Nath Mahajan, as well as the principles concerning rent-default provisions in Ram Chand v. Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., Shyamcharan Sharma v. Dharamdass, and Ram Murti v. Bhola Nath.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession of premises from a tenant.
predicates.defence_struck_for_rent_default: The court struck out the tenant’s defence after the tenant failed to comply with rent-payment or deposit requirements.

issues.definition: When a tenant’s defence is struck out for rent default in a suit for possession, the tenant may generally test the landlord’s case through limited participation.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an available defence does not by itself require a court to decree a landlord’s claim for possession.
material_facts: A landlord sought possession of premises from a tenant in a suit governed by tenancy legislation.
The tenant’s defence against delivery of possession had been struck out.
The court had to decide whether the absence of a defence required a decree without independently assessing the landlord’s case.
issues.conclusion: The court is not required to grant a decree automatically because the tenant’s defence has been struck out or a written statement has not been filed; the landlord must still establish entitlement to relief.
issues.legal_principle: The basic principle that a plaintiff must prove the plaintiff’s case applies even where the defendant does not appear or cannot present a defence. Order VIII rules 1, 5(2), and 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure do not make a decree automatic merely because a written statement is absent; they leave the court discretion as to the appropriate course. The Court also relied on K.K. Chari v. R.H. Seshadri and Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna for the requirement that the court satisfy itself that the conditions for eviction are met.

predicates.tenant_eviction_suit: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession of premises from a tenant.
predicates.defence_unavailable_or_absent: The tenant could not present a defence because the defence had been struck out or no written statement was filed.

issues.definition: In a tenant-eviction proceeding, the absence of an available defence does not itself require the court to grant possession to the landlord.
